title: Desk Booking System for Hybrid Teams: A Full Guide
summary: Find out how a desk booking system for hybrid teams streamlines office space, supports flexible work, and makes in-office collaboration simple and stress-free.
body_text: Your office is one of your biggest expenses, so paying for rows of empty desks simply doesn’t make sense in a hybrid world. Yet, without clear data, it’s hard to know if you have too much space, not enough, or just the wrong kind. Making smart, cost-effective decisions about your real estate requires understanding how your team actually uses the office. This is where a desk booking system for hybrid teams becomes an invaluable strategic tool. It provides the concrete analytics you need to stop guessing and start optimizing your workplace, ensuring every square foot serves a purpose and supports your team’s productivity. Key Takeaways Desk booking is a strategic move, not just an admin tool : It provides the data to use your office space more efficiently, saving money, while also helping teams coordinate in-person days for better collaboration. Focus on a system your team will actually use : The best tools integrate directly into platforms like Slack or Teams , removing the friction of learning a new app and making adoption almost effortless. Always start with a trial run : Before committing, test your top choice with a small group to see if it truly fits your workflow. This ensures you select a flexible system that provides useful data and genuinely supports your team's needs. What is a Desk Booking System ? Think of a desk booking system as a simple reservation tool for your office. Instead of booking a hotel room, your team members book a desk, a meeting room, or even a parking spot for the day. It’s a straightforward way to manage who is coming into the office and when, which is essential for any company that has adopted a hybrid or flexible work model. Gone are the days of assigned seating for everyone; today’s offices need to be more fluid. A hot desk booking system removes the guesswork and chaos that can come with a flexible workplace. It provides a clear, real-time view of what spaces are available, so employees don't have to wander around searching for a place to work. For managers and leadership, it offers valuable insight into how the office is actually being used. This data can help you make smarter decisions about your real estate footprint, potentially saving significant costs. At its core, a desk booking system is about making your office work for your people, not the other way around. How Does Desk Booking Work? The process is incredibly simple. An employee decides they want to work from the office on a certain day. They open an app or, even better, use a tool directly within Slack or Microsoft Teams, and see a list or map of available desks. Many systems also show what amenities come with each desk, like dual monitors or a standing option. With just a few clicks, they can reserve their spot for the day or week. This approach, often called "hot desking" or "desk hoteling," gives everyone the freedom to choose a workspace that fits their needs for that specific day. Why Your Hybrid Team Needs One For a hybrid team, a desk booking system isn't just a nice-to-have, it's a necessity. It ensures your office space is used efficiently, so you aren't paying for rows of empty desks. It also empowers your team by giving them the autonomy to plan their workweeks with effective hybrid work software . Employees can easily coordinate in-office days with their colleagues, making face-to-face collaboration more intentional and productive. This simple tool helps eliminate the anxiety of not knowing if you'll find a spot, making the office a more welcoming and organized place for everyone. What Makes a Great Desk Booking System? When you start looking at desk booking systems, you’ll notice they all promise to make hybrid work easier. But what separates a truly great system from one that just adds another task to your team’s plate? The best tools aren't just about booking a spot; they’re about creating a better office experience. A great system feels less like a rigid set of rules and more like a helpful guide for your team's day. The right hybrid work software should be simple, smart, and slot right into your company's existing workflow. It needs to solve problems, not create new ones. From an employee’s first booking to the reports you review at the end of the month, every feature should have a clear purpose. It’s about finding a tool that empowers your team with autonomy while giving you the oversight needed to manage your space effectively. A system that is hard to use will be ignored, and one that doesn't provide useful data is just a glorified calendar. The goal is to find a balanced solution that serves both employees and management. Let’s walk through the key features that make a desk booking system something your team will thank you for. An Interface Your Team Will Actually Use If a desk booking system is clunky or confusing, your team simply won’t use it. The most critical feature is a user-friendly interface that makes finding and booking a desk take seconds, not minutes. Think about it: the goal is to reduce friction, not add another complicated piece of software to learn. A system that feels intuitive encourages everyone to participate, which is essential for the tool to be effective. When the process is as easy as sending a message, adoption happens naturally, and you get the data you need to manage your space well. Seamless Integration with Your Current Tools The best desk booking software doesn’t force your team to open yet another app. Instead, it meets them where they already work every day. Look for a system that integrates directly into your primary communication tools, like Slack or Microsoft Teams. When booking a desk is just a command or a click away within a platform your team already has open, it becomes a seamless part of their routine. This approach removes the barrier of a separate login and makes the whole process feel effortless. You can explore integrations to see how a system can fit into your existing tech stack. Real-Time Desk Availability There’s nothing more frustrating than booking a desk online only to arrive at the office and find someone else sitting there. A great desk booking system provides a real-time, accurate view of what’s available. This means employees can confidently reserve a spot before they even leave home, knowing it will be ready for them. This feature is the foundation of an effective hot desk booking setup. It prevents double bookings, eliminates confusion, and gives everyone a clear picture of who is in the office and where they are, which is perfect for planning collaborative work. Insightful Reports and Analytics How do you know if your office space is truly working for your team? A great desk booking system gives you the data to answer that question. It should offer clear reports and analytics on desk usage, peak office days, and popular areas. This information is invaluable for making smart decisions about your workplace. You can see which spaces are in high demand and which are sitting empty, allowing you to reconfigure your layout to better match how your team actually works. These insights help you optimize your real estate and create an office that people genuinely want to come to. Customization to Fit Your Office Every office is unique, so your desk booking system should be flexible enough to match your specific layout and policies. Whether you have designated quiet zones, team neighborhoods, or specific desks with special equipment, the software should let you reflect that. The ability to customize office maps or label desks with important details helps employees find the right spot for their needs. This level of personalization makes the office easier to use, especially for new hires or employees who don't come in every day. It ensures the system supports your company culture, not the other way around. The Benefits of a Desk Booking System Adopting a desk booking system isn't just about adding another tool to your tech stack. It’s about fundamentally improving how your office runs for everyone involved. From saving money on real estate to making your employees’ lives easier, the right system can solve some of the biggest hybrid work headaches. It transforms your office from a place people have to be into a place they want to be, fostering collaboration and flexibility without the administrative chaos. Let's look at some of the key benefits you can expect. Use Your Office Space Smarter (and Save Money) Your office is one of your biggest expenses, so paying for empty desks just doesn't make sense. A hot desk booking system gives you a clear picture of how your space is actually being used. By tracking which desks are booked and when, you get real data on your busiest days and most popular areas. This insight is invaluable. It helps you make informed decisions about your office layout, whether that means reconfiguring a floor plan, getting rid of excess space, or even moving to a smaller office that better fits your team’s needs. You stop guessing and start making strategic choices that can significantly reduce your real estate costs. Give Your Team the Flexibility They Crave Flexibility is the cornerstone of a successful hybrid model. Employees want the autonomy to choose a workspace that suits their tasks for the day, whether it's a quiet corner for focused work or a collaborative zone near their team. A desk booking system empowers them to do just that. It removes the uncertainty of finding a spot and gives them control over their in-office experience. This simple act of providing choice shows you trust your team and respect their individual work styles, which goes a long way in building a positive and productive company culture. It’s a key part of making your hybrid work software work for people, not the other way around. Make In-Office Collaboration Effortless One of the biggest challenges of hybrid work is making sure in-office days are actually collaborative. There’s nothing worse than commuting into the office only to find your teammates are all at home. A desk booking system makes it easy for teams to coordinate their schedules. Team members can see who’s planning to be in the office and book desks near each other, turning office days into intentional, productive sessions. This is especially helpful for project kick-offs, brainstorming meetings, or just reconnecting in person. It helps your flex office software support teamwork, ensuring that time spent in the office is time well spent. Cut Down on Admin Work Manually managing desk reservations with spreadsheets or messy Slack channels is a recipe for headaches. It’s time-consuming for office managers and frustrating for employees. A desk booking system automates the entire process. It handles reservations, sends reminders, and provides a single source of truth for who is where and when. This frees up your administrative and HR teams from tedious manual tracking, allowing them to focus on more impactful work. For employees, it means finding and booking a desk takes seconds, not a long email chain. It streamlines the logistics so everyone can focus on their actual jobs. Common Hybrid Work Problems a Booking System Solves The shift to hybrid work has been great for flexibility, but it’s also introduced a few new logistical headaches. Without the right systems in place, your office can feel chaotic, with employees unsure where to sit and managers struggling to get a clear picture of who’s coming in. A desk booking system isn't just a nice-to-have tool; it’s a practical solution to the everyday friction points that can make or break your hybrid model. It brings order to the office, making in-person days more intentional and productive for everyone involved. These systems directly address the common pain points of a flexible workplace. They tackle everything from the morning scramble for a good desk to the bigger picture of managing office capacity and understanding space utilization. Instead of guessing how many people will show up on a Tuesday, you have clear data. Instead of employees feeling anxious about finding a spot, they feel empowered and prepared. A booking system smooths out the wrinkles of a flexible schedule, turning potential chaos into coordinated collaboration and ensuring your office is a place people actually want to be. It transforms your physical space from a source of uncertainty into a reliable resource for your team. End the "Is This Desk Taken?" Confusion There’s nothing worse than arriving at the office ready to work, only to spend the first 15 minutes wandering around looking for an open spot. The awkward shuffle past colleagues and the hesitant "Is anyone sitting here?" question can kill productivity before the day even begins. A hot desk booking system eliminates this uncertainty completely. By allowing employees to reserve a specific desk before they even commute, it ensures everyone has a designated place to work. This simple act of booking a desk provides clarity, saves valuable time, and helps your team start their office days feeling settled and prepared. Stop Overbooking and "Ghost" Desks Have you ever walked through an office that feels empty, only to find that every desk has a laptop or notebook on it? This is the "ghost desk" problem. It often happens when employees, worried about finding a spot, book a desk "just in case" and then don't show up. This leads to frustration and inefficient use of your space. A booking system provides a real-time view of who has booked and who has checked in. This transparency discourages overbooking and makes it easy for others to see which desks are truly available, creating a fairer and more efficient system for the entire team. Reduce Office-Day Anxiety For many employees, the biggest hurdle to a successful office day is the unknown. Will I find a quiet spot for my focus work? Can I sit near my team for our project collaboration? This uncertainty can create a low level of anxiety that makes coming into the office feel like a chore. A desk booking system gives your team autonomy and control over their environment. It allows them to choose a space that suits their needs for the day, which can significantly reduce stress. This simple tool helps transform office days from a source of anxiety into a positive, intentional part of their hybrid work software experience. Easily Manage Office Policies Implementing and enforcing office policies in a flexible environment can be a challenge for managers. How do you manage capacity limits, assign specific neighborhoods to teams, or prevent the same people from booking the best desks every day? A good booking system helps you manage these policies without constant manual oversight. You can set booking rules, create designated zones, and get data on space usage to make informed decisions. This ensures your flex office software aligns with company goals while still meeting the needs of your employees, making office management much simpler and more effective. What Are Your Options? Types of Desk Booking Systems Once you start looking for a desk booking system, you'll notice they come in a few different flavors. Understanding the main types will help you narrow down what’s right for your team and your office. Most tools fall into one of three categories: standalone platforms, all-in-one suites, or systems that work inside the communication apps you already use. Each has its own approach, so let's break down what that means for you and your employees. Standalone Booking Platforms Think of these as the specialists. Standalone booking platforms are designed to do one thing really well: reserve spaces. Employees use a separate app or website to see what desks are available and book a spot for the day. The interface is usually straightforward and focused entirely on the booking process, which makes it a dedicated hot desk booking system . While this simplicity can be appealing, it also means adding another tool to your team's tech stack. This requires everyone to remember another login and learn a new system, which can sometimes be a barrier to getting the whole team on board with using it regularly. All-in-One Workplace Suites These are the big, comprehensive platforms that aim to be your single source for all things workplace management. Desk booking is just one piece of the puzzle. These suites often include features for resource management, detailed analytics, and even employee engagement tools, creating a complete hybrid work software solution. The main draw is having everything under one roof, which can provide a holistic view of your office operations. However, these systems can be complex and costly. You might find yourself paying for a lot of features your team doesn't actually need, and they still require employees to adopt yet another separate piece of software. Tools That Live in Your Communication Apps This newer approach meets your team right where they are: in apps like Slack or Microsoft Teams. Instead of making employees switch to a different platform, these tools integrate directly into the communication hubs they use all day. Booking a desk becomes as simple as sending a message or clicking a button within a familiar environment. This convenience is a game-changer for adoption rates. When the tool is part of an existing workflow, people are far more likely to use it consistently. Exploring these integrations shows how it removes the friction of learning a new system and keeps the process of coming into the office easy and stress-free. What's the Investment? A Look at Desk Booking Costs When you start looking at desk booking systems, the price can seem all over the place. The good news is that there’s a solution for almost every budget. The key is to understand what you’re paying for and how different pricing models work. Investing in the right tool isn’t just about the software; it’s about creating a better office experience for your team. Let’s break down the costs so you can find a system that fits your company’s needs and budget perfectly. Understanding Pricing Models Most desk booking software operates on a subscription basis, typically with a per-user, per-month fee. This model is great because it scales with your company. As you grow, you can add more users, and if you need to downsize, you can adjust your plan accordingly. You’ll also find tiered plans that bundle features together. A basic tier might offer simple desk booking, while premium tiers could include analytics, meeting room booking, and advanced integrations. It’s worth taking a close look at the different pricing plans available to see which features are included at each level. This helps you avoid paying for tools you don’t need. What Influences the Price Tag? Several factors determine the final cost of a desk booking system. The most obvious one is the number of employees who will be using it. Beyond headcount, the range of features plays a big role. A simple tool for hot desking will cost less than a comprehensive platform that also manages meeting rooms and office parking . The depth of integrations also affects the price. A system that seamlessly connects with the tools your team already uses, like Slack or Microsoft Teams, provides more value and often comes with a higher price tag. Think about what’s essential for your team to work productively and choose a system that matches those needs. The Importance of a Free Trial Before you commit to any subscription, taking the software for a test drive is essential. A free trial lets you see how the system works in your actual office environment. It’s your chance to check if the interface is truly user-friendly and if your team will adopt it without a lot of friction. This is especially important for hybrid teams that need a simple way to coordinate their in-office days. You can test the core features, see how it integrates with your current workflow, and get direct feedback from your employees. With a tool like Officely , you can start a free trial for up to five employees to see the benefits firsthand before making a financial commitment. How to Choose the Right Desk Booking System You're sold on the idea of a desk booking system. But with so many options out there, how do you pick the one that won't just become another ignored piece of software? It comes down to finding a tool that fits your team's unique rhythm. Let's walk through what to look for, how to launch it successfully, and what mistakes to sidestep along the way. title: How Businesses Can Recycle Bulk Cardboard in Salt Lake City, UT
summary: Learn how recycling in Salt Lake City helps businesses manage bulk cardboard efficiently. Discover practical solutions to keep operations organized.
body_text: For businesses in Salt Lake City, corrugated packaging is part of daily operations. Products arrive in boxes, orders ship out in boxes, and cardboard builds up quickly across warehouses and distribution centers. Without a clear system in place, managing that volume can become a challenge. That is where recycling in Salt Lake City becomes essential. With the right approach, businesses can handle bulk cardboard efficiently while keeping operations organized and materials in use. Why Bulk Cardboard Recycling Matters In high-volume environments, cardboard is more than occasional waste. It is a constant output tied directly to how a business operates. Facilities that prioritize recycling in the Salt Lake City area can: Keep workspaces clear and efficient Reduce clutter in high-traffic areas Improve safety on warehouse floors Minimize waste sent to landfills Support sustainability goals across operations Recycling helps turn used cardboard into a manageable resource instead of a growing operational issue. Understanding Bulk Cardboard in Commercial Settings Bulk cardboard typically comes from corrugated packaging used in shipping and storage. This includes: Shipping boxes Corrugated sheets Packaging inserts Large volume product containers These materials, often referred to as OCC (Old Corrugated Containers), are highly recyclable and can be reused multiple times to create new packaging. Businesses that participate in Salt Lake City recycling efforts help make sure this material stays in circulation rather than being discarded or sent to landfill. Setting Up an Efficient Cardboard Recycling System Creating a reliable recycling process starts with understanding how cardboard moves through your facility. 1. Identify Key Collection Points Look for areas where cardboard accumulates most often, such as: Receiving docks Packing stations Production areas Placing recycling collection stations in these locations makes it easier for teams to dispose of materials properly. 2. Establish Clear Collection Areas Designated recycling zones help keep cardboard organized and prevent it from mixing with general waste. Clear signage and easy access encourage consistent use. 3. Prepare Cardboard for Recycling Flattening boxes reduces the amount of space they take up and makes handling easier. Keeping materials clean and dry is also important to ensure they can be processed effectively. For large-volume operations, equipment such as balers and compactors can compress cardboard into compact bundles for you, improving storage and transportation efficiency. Choosing the Right Recycling Solution Not all recycling setups are the same. The right solution depends on your facility’s size, volume, and workflow. When evaluating options for recycling in Salt Lake City, consider: Pickup frequency High-volume operations may need frequent collection to keep materials moving, so it's important to find a recycling partner who can match your requirements. Material volume The amount of cardboard generated will determine whether simple collection containers or equipment like balers and compactors are needed. Space availability Facilities with limited space may require compact solutions, while larger operations can support dedicated recycling areas. Operational fit Recycling should integrate smoothly into existing processes without slowing down productivity. Selecting the right setup ensures that recycling supports your operation rather than complicating it. Integrating Recycling Into Daily Operations The most effective recycling systems are built into everyday workflows. When cardboard is handled consistently at each stage, it doesn't become a problem later. Businesses can improve their approach to recycling in Salt Lake City by: Sorting boxes and materials by type immediately after use Keeping recycling stations close to work areas Training employees on proper handling Maintaining clean, organized collection zones These habits help create a steady flow of materials from use to collection. How Recycling Supports the Packaging Cycle Cardboard recycling is part of a larger recycling ecosystem that keeps materials in use. When businesses recycle corrugated packaging, the fiber is recovered and reused to create new products. This cycle includes: Producing packaging from new, renewable fiber as well as recovered fiber Using boxes to transport goods and conduct daily operations Collecting and recycling used cardboard Turning recovered fiber into new packaging again By participating in recycling in Salt Lake City, businesses help support this ongoing, circular cycle and extend the life of renewable materials. Building a Long-Term Recycling Strategy Recycling bulk cardboard is not a one-time effort. It requires a system that works consistently over time and adapts as your business grows. A strong recycling strategy helps businesses: Maintain organized and efficient facilities Manage high volumes of material Reduce unnecessary waste Support responsible resource use For businesses in Salt Lake City, setting up a reliable recycling system ensures that cardboard is handled efficiently and contributes to a broader effort to keep materials in circulation. Supporting Efficient Operations Through Recycling Managing bulk cardboard does not have to be a challenge. With the right processes, equipment, and support in place, recycling becomes a seamless part of daily operations. title: H2@Work Employee Spotlight: Damon Curtis
summary: Damon serves as Manager of Data Systems within Plug’s Service Group. He leads the enterprise data infrastructure that supports both GenFuel and GenDrive operations.
body_text: Damon serves as Manager of Data Systems within Plug’s Service Group. He leads the enterprise data infrastructure that supports both GenFuel and GenDrive operations. His work includes overseeing fueling network control systems, condition-based monitoring platforms, analytics environments, and the GenDrive fuel cell data ecosystem. Damon also manages the service data portal that is evolving into the next generation Field Service Management platform, helping improve uptime, safety, and operational efficiency across the hydrogen network. From Technical Integration to Hydrogen Infrastructure Damon came to Plug with a background in technical integrations and problem solving. After owning and operating his own business, he experienced the shift from analog to digital control systems firsthand. Designing and installing those systems gave him a deep understanding of both field operations and system architecture. That experience naturally led him to an environment where technology, infrastructure, and operational performance intersect. Growing Alongside the Hydrogen Industry Damon has spent more than a decade at Plug. When he first joined, hydrogen fueling infrastructure was still new and evolving. The early days of the first GenFuel systems stand out as one of the most extraordinary periods of his career. He remembers stepping into the hydrogen field for the first time and learning how every component had to align, from storage and compression to dispensing, fuel cells, service operations, and data systems. Watching that ecosystem take shape gave him a front row seat to the growth of an entirely new energy platform. Facing Complex Challenges with Determination Damon believes building an energy solution that can impact the world is naturally complex. The hydrogen industry is shaped by shifting markets, evolving regulations, and rapid technological change. Through those challenges he has learned that progress often comes from solving the problem directly in front of you and trusting that steady improvement matters. He credits Plug’s entrepreneurial culture for encouraging people to take ownership, push through adversity, and support each other along the way. Excited by the Journey of Learning While the long-term potential of hydrogen and fuel cells is exciting, Damon says the most rewarding part is the challenge of learning and problem solving. When he first joined Plug, he had no experience with fuel cells or liquid hydrogen systems. Over time, through hands on experience and constant learning, he built deep knowledge in technology that could shape the future of global energy. A Philosophy of Building What Matters Damon approaches life with a simple philosophy. Build things that matter. Whether it is systems, teams, or relationships, he believes in creating lasting value and leaving every environment stronger than he found it. Memories from the Journey Damon loves family vacations and the stories that come from them. One trip stands out, traveling from Kentucky to Myrtle Beach in a rented motor home. As the engine sputtered and backfired along the highway, Damon and his cousins laughed uncontrollably from the back of the camper. He may not remember much about the beach itself, but he still remembers the ride. For Damon, it is a reminder that sometimes the best memories come from the unexpected moments along the journey.

title: Byrna's Lawsuit Against California's Ban on Chemical Rounds
summary: Byrna challenges California’s ban on pepper projectile rounds in a federal lawsuit. Learn how this case could impact less-lethal self-defense laws, expand access to non-lethal options, and set a nationwide legal precedent.
body_text: Byrna Challenges California Ban on Less-Lethal Pepper Projectiles A high-profile legal battle is unfolding in California as Byrna Technologies moves forward with a lawsuit challenging the state’s ban on chemical agent projectiles , including pepper-based rounds. The case has the potential to influence how less-lethal self-defense tools are regulated—not just in California, but across the United States. Current Legal Status in California Despite ongoing litigation, it is important to note that Byrna launchers and kinetic ammunition remain legal in California . In fact, California represents one of the largest markets for less-lethal launchers, reflecting strong consumer demand for alternative self-defense options. The legal challenge specifically targets restrictions on pepper and chemical projectile rounds , which are currently treated differently than other self-defense tools. This distinction has raised questions among advocates who argue that less-lethal technologies should be more broadly accessible. The Core of the Lawsuit The lawsuit, filed in federal court in San Diego, seeks to clarify how less-lethal tools are categorized under the law. At the center of the argument is the inconsistency in how California regulates defensive products. While residents can legally purchase firearms and traditional pepper spray, certain projectile-based chemical deterrents remain restricted. Supporters of the case also point to previous rulings by the Supreme Court of the United States , which have recognized that the Second Amendment extends to commonly used tools for lawful self-defense—including some non-lethal weapons. Potential National Impact If successful, the case could establish an important legal precedent, potentially influencing how other states approach similar restrictions. Expanding access to less-lethal tools could provide individuals with more options to protect themselves without resorting to deadly force. A Focus on Safety and Access The broader conversation surrounding this case centers on public safety, personal protection, and responsible access to defensive tools . Less-lethal technologies are often viewed as a way to de-escalate dangerous situations while reducing the risk of permanent harm. As the case progresses, it will continue to draw attention from lawmakers, legal experts, and individuals interested in the future of self-defense rights. The outcome may help shape the evolving landscape of less-lethal technology and its role in modern personal protection.

body_text: 2026 Mar. 02 PDF THOMASVILLE, Ga., Mar. 2, 2026 — Flowers Foods, Inc. (NYSE: FLO) today announced that Michelle Lorge has been appointed president of Simple Mills. Lorge will report directly to Ryals McMullian, chairman and CEO of Flowers Foods. She succeeds Katlin Smith, founder and CEO of Simple Mills, who has made a personal decision to step down to spend more time with her family and on philanthropic interests, and will continue with the company in an advisory capacity. Michelle Lorge Katlin Smith “Michelle has been instrumental in shaping Simple Mills into the mission-driven, high-growth brand it is today,” said McMullian. “Her deep understanding of the business, strong leadership skills, and unwavering commitment to the company’s purpose make her exceptionally well-suited to lead Simple Mills into its next chapter. We are grateful to Katlin for her vision and leadership and look forward to her continued support in an advisory role.” Lorge, an 11-year veteran of Simple Mills, has built the brand alongside Smith, transforming the company from an early-stage startup into a leading natural cracker, cookie, bar, and baking mix brand with distribution in more than 30,000 stores nationwide. Most recently she served as chief marketing, innovation, and mission officer, where she led product innovation, built a purpose-driven marketing organization, and advanced wellness and sustainability initiatives that have helped redefine industry standards. Lorge joined Simple Mills in 2015 as one of the brand’s first employees. Prior to joining Simple Mills, Lorge spent more than a decade at Kraft Foods where she led brand marketing and product innovation for Philadelphia, A.1., Grey Poupon, and Cool Whip. “I am honored to step into this role and continue the incredible work Katlin started,” said Lorge. “Simple Mills was founded on a belief that food can have a profound impact on human and planetary health, and that belief continues to inspire everything we do. I look forward to continuing to work with our talented team to advance our people and planet mission and broaden our impact to ignite meaningful change in the food industry and beyond.” Smith founded Simple Mills in 2012 after recognizing the transformative power of food in improving overall well-being. Under her leadership, the company grew into a category-leading brand carried by major retailers including Whole Foods, Sprouts, Target, Walmart, and Costco, alongside a strong e-commerce presence on Amazon. She has been widely recognized for her entrepreneurial achievements, receiving honors such as Forbes 30 Under 30, Inc. 30 Under 30, and Progressive Grocer’s Top Woman in Grocery. “Building Simple Mills has been one of the greatest privileges of my life,” said Katlin Smith. “Michelle has been by my side shaping Simple Mills for many years and is deeply aligned with the mission and values that define who we are. I have full confidence in her ability to lead Simple Mills into the future.” About Flowers Foods Headquartered in Thomasville, Ga., Flowers Foods, Inc. title: The future of vacation rental technology and AI: beyond 2026
summary: Is your portfolio ready for the next era of hospitality? Explore the essential AI tools and tech strategies needed to dominate the market beyond 2026.
body_text: The future of vacation rental technology and AI: beyond 2026 by Josh Genuth , Senior Content Writer | March 12, 2026 Reading time: 4 minutes Share Josh Genuth , Senior Content Writer Share The vacation rental industry has moved past the era of simple listing management. By 2026, the gap between tech-enabled operators and manual hosts will be significant — and widening. You face rising guest expectations and tightening local regulations, making efficiency a survival requirement rather than a secondary goal. Artificial intelligence is now the core engine of hospitality, handling repetitive tasks to free up your schedule for property acquisition and high-level management. Data governs every decision from cleaning schedules to nightly rates. The most successful operators will integrate technology deeply into their daily operations, using their tech stacks to protect margins and prevent the burnout that comes from outdated manual methods. TL;DR AI-driven communication handles the majority of guest inquiries without human intervention. Hyper-local dynamic pricing adjusts for micro-events like neighborhood street fairs and local festivals. Predictive maintenance identifies failing appliances before they break and ruin a guest stay. Unified platforms replace fragmented toolsets to prevent data silos and double bookings. Automated guest screening reduces liability risk without requiring manual background checks. Smart home integration is increasingly expected by insurers and guests alike, supporting both security and operational efficiency. The rising hurdles of property management Regulation and operational costs are the primary threats to your margin. Local governments are increasing licensing requirements and caps, necessitating systems that track compliance automatically to avoid fines. Labor for cleaning and maintenance takes a significant portion of revenue, meaning every minute of staff time must be accounted for to reach the break-even point on your mortgage. Guest expectations are reaching hotel standards for instant answers and perfect cleanliness. A single missed message can lead to a four-star review, which lowers your ranking on major booking channels. You cannot scale a business or maintain profitability on manual replies alone. Use AI to manage daily operations AI operates as your 24/7 operations manager by monitoring inboxes and prioritizing urgent maintenance issues like water leaks over general requests. Predictive analytics also remove the guesswork from property acquisition by using booking data to project future returns and minimize financial risk. While these tools increase efficiency, review your automated templates to ensure they sound professional and direct rather than like a corporate handbook. Use autonomous communication to handle inquiries Stop typing the same directions to the lockbox. Use Guesty ReplyAI to generate instant, context-aware responses to guest questions. This tool learns your specific house rules and local recommendations so you maintain control while the software handles the high-volume messaging. Protect margins through intelligent pricing Fixed weekend rates are pretty much dead. You must capture every cent of market demand by using automated pricing tools that analyze competitor occupancy and local events in real-time. This prevents you from leaving money on the table during peak dates and fills occupancy gaps during the slow season. title: Does Renters Insurance Cover Dog Bites? Coverage, Exclusions, and What Renters Should Check
summary: Does renters insurance cover dog bites? Often yes, but breed restrictions, bite history, and policy exclusions can change the answer. Learn what to check.
body_text: Many renters assume the answer is simple: if a dog bites someone, renters insurance pays. In reality, it is often yes, but not always . Most renters policies include personal liability coverage, and several major insurers publicly say that dog-bite liability may be covered, but coverage can change based on the insurer, the policy form, the state, the dog’s breed, and whether the dog has a prior bite history. That detail matters because dog-related injury claims are expensive. The Insurance Information Institute and State Farm reported that U.S. dog-related injury claims reached 22,658 in 2024, with total claim payouts of $1.57 billion and an average cost per claim of $69,272 . The short answer Renters insurance often covers dog bites through personal liability coverage, and sometimes medical payments to others, but there are important exclusions. Progressive says dog bites are covered in many instances under bodily injury liability, GEICO says coverage can apply if the policy includes dog liability coverage and the dog’s breed is not excluded, and Lemonade says dog-bite liability is generally covered unless the dog has a bite history or falls into a high-risk category under the policy. How dog-bite coverage usually works In a standard renters policy, the most relevant sections are usually personal liability and medical payments to others . Personal liability can help with bodily injury, property damage, legal defense, court costs, and settlements when you are legally responsible. Medical payments to others is a smaller no-fault coverage that may help with reasonable medical bills for an injured guest, depending on the policy. GEICO, Allstate, State Farm, and Progressive all describe these coverages in broadly similar ways. A practical way to think about it is this: Situation Usually covered? Why Your dog bites a guest and you are legally responsible Often yes This is typically a personal liability claim Your dog injures a guest and they need immediate treatment Sometimes Medical payments to others may apply, depending on the policy The injured person sues you Often yes, if covered Liability coverage may help with legal defense and damages up to limits Your dog damages someone else’s property Often yes, if covered Property damage liability may apply Your dog damages your couch, TV, or belongings Usually no Your own property damage from your pet is generally excluded Your dog damages your apartment or rental unit Usually no, or very limited Pet-caused damage to the unit is often not what renters insurance is designed to cover Your dog bites someone in your household Usually no Household/resident injuries are commonly excluded from this part of coverage Your dog’s own vet bills after an incident No That is pet insurance territory, not renters liability coverage This table is a plain-English summary of current public guidance from major insurers and policy forms. Dog bites are not always only a “home” problem Another detail renters often miss: liability can matter away from your apartment too . Lemonade gives a public example of a dog injuring another dog at a dog park, and GEICO and Progressive both describe renters liability in a way that is not limited only to something happening inside the unit. The exact scope still depends on the policy, but dog-bite claims are not always confined to your living room. Why the answer can become “no” This is the part many articles skip: the declarations page, endorsements, and exclusions can completely change the result. Lemonade’s public HO-4 sample form includes a Canine Liability Exclusion Endorsement that says Coverage E (Personal Liability) and Coverage F (Medical Payments to Others) do not apply to bodily injury or property damage caused by listed breeds or breed mixes, trained guard dogs, or any dog with a prior bite history documented by an insurance claim, police report, or civil complaint. That same sample endorsement also says the exclusion does not apply to certain guide, hearing, or physically disabled assistance dogs. That is not unique to one insurer. GEICO says many renters policies include breed restrictions and notes that commonly excluded breeds may include Pit Bulls, Rottweilers, and Dobermans. Liberty Mutual likewise says some insurers exclude breeds such as Pit Bulls, Rottweilers, Doberman Pinschers, German Shepherds, Chow Chows, Akitas, wolf hybrids, and Alaskan Malamutes. Lemonade’s FAQ says coverage generally does not apply if the dog has a bite history or is categorized as a high-risk breed under the policy. At the same time, breed rules are not universal . The Insurance Information Institute says some insurers will not insure certain breeds, others decide case by case, and some do not ask breed at all when writing or renewing coverage. State Farm also emphasizes that “it’s not the breed” in its public dog-bite safety content. So the right takeaway is not “all insurers ban the same dogs,” but rather “you have to read your own policy.” What renters insurance usually does not cover Even if your policy does cover third-party dog-bite liability, that does not mean it covers every dog-related expense. GEICO says renters insurance generally does not cover damage your dog causes to your own belongings or rental unit, and injuries to people living in your household are also typically excluded. Liberty Mutual similarly says pet liability insurance for renters does not cover damage to your own stuff, and State Farm notes that most renters policies do not cover damage to your personal belongings caused by a pet. It also does not replace pet insurance. Liberty Mutual’s renters page says renters insurance does not cover pets themselves and that you would need a separate pet policy for your animal’s own health expenses. Lemonade makes the same distinction: renters insurance can help with pet-related liability, while pet insurance is for your pet’s veterinary care. What to check in your policy before assuming you are covered Before relying on renters insurance for a dog-bite claim, check these five things: Your liability limit. State Farm says the typical renters policy offers $100,000 in liability coverage, but serious dog-bite claims can exceed that quickly. Whether medical payments to others is included and how much it is. This coverage can help with smaller bills even when fault is not fully established, but limits are usually modest. Pet or canine endorsements/exclusions. Do not stop at the declarations page. Read the endorsements section for breed lists, prior-bite exclusions, or special pet underwriting language. Lemonade’s sample form is a good reminder of how much one endorsement can change. Whether your dog has a bite history. Public carrier guidance from Lemonade and Liberty Mutual makes clear that prior incidents are a major red flag for coverage. Whether you need umbrella coverage. Allstate, Liberty Mutual, and State Farm all publicly describe umbrella coverage as an added layer when liability claims get large, including scenarios involving dog bites. A simple, accurate rule of thumb If your dog bites someone, renters insurance may help with the injured person’s medical bills, legal expenses, and liability damages. But that answer only holds if the dog is not excluded, the claim falls within the policy’s liability terms, and no endorsement removes coverage. Public carrier language today consistently points to the same pattern: coverage is possible, exclusions are common, and policy wording matters. FAQ Does renters insurance cover dog bites to guests? Often yes, through personal liability coverage, and sometimes through medical payments to others for smaller immediate expenses, depending on the policy. Does renters insurance cover dog bites from any breed? No. Some insurers use breed restrictions, some use case-by-case underwriting, and some may exclude dogs with prior bite history. Does renters insurance cover my dog’s own injuries or vet bills? No. That is generally outside renters insurance and belongs under pet insurance instead. Does renters insurance cover damage my dog causes to my own furniture or apartment? Usually not. Public insurer guidance generally says pet-caused damage to your own stuff or rental unit is not what renters insurance is designed to cover. Coverage, exclusions, endorsements, underwriting rules, and breed restrictions vary by insurer, policy, and state. Review your own policy documents for the exact terms that apply. title: The Overlooked Importance of Battery Storage
summary: Building North America's only fully integrated, localized and environmentally sustainable battery materials park.
body_text: The Overlooked Importance of Battery Storage Battery storage has become a foundational pillar of the energy transition, even if it rarely commands the same attention as electric vehicles or renewable generation. As electrification expands across transport, consumer electronics, and grid-scale energy systems, the ability to store energy reliably, safely, and at scale is becoming just as critical as the ability to generate it. Meeting this growing storage demand depends on a diverse ecosystem of battery technologies and materials. While lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries dominate many stationary storage applications, other lithium-ion chemistries remain essential for use cases that demand higher energy density, performance, and compact design. In these systems, materials like cobalt continue to play an important role in shaping how batteries perform, how long they last, and how safely they operate. Understanding battery storage, therefore, goes beyond identifying the most widely used chemistry. It requires examining how different materials support different storage needs and where cobalt fits within an increasingly diversified battery landscape. Why Cobalt Matters in Battery Storage Lithium-ion batteries store and release energy through the movement of lithium ions between the anode and the cathode, with the cathode composition playing a decisive role in energy density, stability, and lifespan. Cobalt has historically been integral to several widely deployed cathode chemistries, particularly those optimized for high energy density. Cobalt helps stabilize the cathode structure during repeated charging and discharging, reducing degradation and the risk of overheating. In practical terms, this enables batteries to store more energy in smaller volumes, operate more safely under demanding conditions, and maintain performance over long lifetimes characteristics that are especially valuable in applications where space, reliability, and durability are critical. These attributes explain why cobalt became a key material during the rapid scaling of lithium-ion batteries over the past decade. As demand surged for batteries that could deliver consistent performance at scale, cobalt-containing chemistries provided a proven solution. While efforts to optimize or reduce cobalt use are accelerating, its contribution to the development of high-performance, long-lasting battery storage remains significant. The Challenges and Shifting Role of Cobalt As battery storage scales globally, the cobalt industry has undergone significant evolution. Because production is geographically concentrated, stakeholders across the value chain have invested in strengthening supply security, diversifying sourcing partnerships, and improving long-term contracting structures to enhance stability and predictability. In parallel, heightened expectations around environmental and social standards have accelerated improvements in transparency and accountability. Producers, governments, and downstream manufacturers have expanded due diligence frameworks, formalized responsible sourcing initiatives, and increased traceability across supply chains. These efforts are reshaping how cobalt is produced and procured, reinforcing higher operational and ethical standards across the industry. At the same time, technological innovation has made cobalt use more efficient. Advances in cathode chemistry have reduced cobalt intensity while preserving its stabilizing and performance benefits, particularly in applications where durability and safety remain critical. Recycling and closed-loop systems are also gaining traction, enabling cobalt recovery and reducing reliance on primary extraction. Together, these developments reflect a broader optimization rather than a phase-out. While lower cobalt intensity can improve cost efficiency and sustainability metrics, maintaining performance, thermal stability, and long cycle life remains essential in many battery applications. As a result, cobalt’s role is becoming more strategic and targeted. Cobalt’s Evolving Place in the Storage Future Battery storage is no longer a supporting technology; it is a backbone of global electrification. As energy systems become more decentralized and increasingly reliant on renewables, reliable storage will continue to shape the pace and effectiveness of the transition. Within this context, cobalt’s role is changing but not disappearing. While alternative chemistries have reduced its dominance in some segments, cobalt remains critical in applications where high performance, safety, and long cycle life are essential. It is increasingly positioned as a transitional, purpose-driven material rather than a default component. The future of battery storage will depend on balanced innovation, scaling capacity while improving sustainability and supply-chain resilience without sacrificing performance. How cobalt is managed through smarter chemistry, responsible sourcing, and recycling will be an important part of meeting the growing demand for dependable energy storage in an electrified world.

title: HIPAA + PCI for Healthcare Billing: Protecting Both PHI and Payment Card Data
summary: What HIPAA PCI compliance requires for healthcare billing pages, from run-time script risks to vendor agreements and unified controls.
body_text: When a patient logs into a billing portal, two of the most heavily regulated data types in the U.S. end up in the same browser session. PHI like health history, insurance providers, and diagnoses, renders right alongside the card entry fields they’ll use to pay. And with them load the third-party scripts that marketing manages. Analytics, heatmaps, A/B testing, conversion tracking. These tools are how growth teams optimize revenue and product teams improve the experience. But the problem is that once they load in a patient’s browser at run-time, they can read everything in that DOM. Including the PHI and the payment fields. Unless someone has deliberately governed what those scripts are allowed to touch, they see everything. That’s the risk both PCI DSS 4.0.1 and OCR under HIPAA are now doubling down on. But they approach it differently, with different controls, different cadences, and different enforcement teeth. This article is about navigating both at once. What you’ll learn Where HIPAA and PCI DSS overlap and where they don’t What run-time visibility actually looks like in practice, and how it maps to PCI DSS 6.4.3, 11.6.1, and OCR’s tracking guidance How to leverage the differences and similarities to unify HIPAA + PCI compliance for healthcare billing Where HIPAA and PCI DSS overlap Although HIPAA and PCI DSS emerged from different policy processes, on healthcare pages, they mitigate the same categories of threat, like unauthorized access, tampering, and e-skimming, with access controls, encryption, audit logging, and vendor agreements The language differs, but both of them demand all of it to reduce the likelihood of compromising sensitive data. Let’s look at the areas where they converge in detail: Access controls to restrict unauthorized use Both frameworks require that only authorized users and software can reach sensitive data. How they implement it differs slightly. HIPAA mandates unique user IDs, automatic logoff, and access controls tied to specific roles. On the other hand, PCI demands least-privilege access, role-based controls, and MFA for anyone with administrative access to the cardholder data environment. However, there are nuances you need to watch out for. Having MFA and RBAC for the systems that store PHI and card data is not enough. HIPAA cares equally about who can access PHI in transit or in ephemeral browser views. Any third-party like tags would need a BAA to justify the data use. Likewise, PCI 4.0.1 pulls scripts running in the consumer’s browser into scope via requirements 6.4.3 and 11.6.1, even when no staff member ever logs into those scripts. And those scripts need to be governed, inventoried, and continuously monitored for changes. Encryption for data at rest and in transit. HIPAA treats encryption as addressable, which means you can implement it where reasonable and appropriate, or document why you didn’t. PCI is more direct and all-encompassing. Strong cryptography for cardholder data in transit over open networks is mandatory. Period. That means, if you design your encryption controls for PCI DSS, you’ll most likely meet HIPAA’s requirements as well. However, what most teams don’t get is that data is decrypted once the customer’s browser receives it. Which means, it can be seen by unauthorized scripts on the website. Both frameworks’ intent extends beyond the wire to what happens after decryption. Audit logging and monitoring HIPAA requires audit controls that record and examine activity in systems containing ePHI. PCI requires detailed logging of access to cardholder data, security events, and administrative actions, with daily review. Centralizing logging across your payment portal stack, like web servers, API gateways, identity providers, and payment microservices, serves both frameworks simultaneously. But logs almost never extend into the browser. The scripts executing in a patient’s session, reading PHI, and hovering over payment fields, leave no trace in a traditional SIEM. Closing that gap requires purpose-built run-time visibility that both frameworks can trust. Vendor agreements HIPAA requires Business Associate Agreements with any vendor that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on your behalf. PCI requires service provider agreements that define compliance responsibilities and evidence expectations like AOCs and attestations. The challenge is that on a payment page, a single vendor often needs to be both. A portal platform that renders patient billing information and hosts payment functionality is simultaneously a business associate and a PCI service provider. Those two contracts get reviewed by different teams, negotiated on different timelines, and rarely align on what happens when something goes wrong in the browser. Incident response and risk assessments Both frameworks require formal risk assessments, documented incident response procedures, and regular testing. HIPAA’s Security Management Process demands an accurate and thorough assessment of risks to ePHI, with ongoing risk management. On the other hand, PCI expects forensic readiness and a documented ability to contain and eradicate compromises in the cardholder data environment. That’s both an overhead and an opportunity. A unified risk analysis covering the payment portal, explicitly modeling threats to both PHI and cardholder data in that shared space, can serve both frameworks at once. Mitigating risks emerging from third-party scripts is a new addition of expectation from both frameworks, though. And that’s where the unified approach matters the most. HIPAA + PCI compliance: Key difference in approach Though they share a common goal of protecting data on healthcare payment pages, the way they prescribe implementation and what data they aim to protect differ. PCI DSS now spells out what “good” looks like for client‑side script governance. It’s prescriptive, and lays clear expectations of controls and policies that should be implemented. HIPAA offers you more flexibility with your implementation. What it does is lay out first principles, mark the boundary you need to respect, and point you towards the outcomes. You still have the option to reason from first principles and translate it into controls to protect ePHI from tracking scripts. Let’s look at these differences closely. PCI DSS 4.0.1 prescribes how you govern the digital experience layer Requirements 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 address protection for browser-based payment pages, targeting the attack surface on the client end. While Requirement 6.4.3 focuses on prevention by mandating that every script on a payment page is authorized, verified, and documented, Requirement 11.6.1 focuses on detection. It requires continuous monitoring and alerts for unauthorized changes to scripts or security-impacting HTTP headers. HIPAA expects the same, without explicitly stating how HIPAA expects you to identify risks emerging from tracking technologies via risk analysis and then take appropriate measures to mitigate them. There is no regulation that explicitly mandates a script inventory or tamper detection for pages that expose PHI. But OCR’s tracking guidance forces you to the same conclusion through risk analysis. If third-party scripts on your portal can access PHI in the DOM and send it to external domains, your risk management program must treat that as a potential unauthorized disclosure. The controls aren’t spelled out. The obligation is. Scope: HIPAA and PCI cover different data types Put simply, PCI primarily includes the cardholder data environment in the scope. That means any webpage or iFrame that receives card data, or any system that stores, processes, or transmits come under PCI’s scope. HIPAA scopes all PHI, in any format, across the covered entity and its business associates. On a payment portal, PCI might formally scope only the endpoints and payment widgets that handle card data. HIPAA scopes the entire portal, including every billing workflow and every tracker that touches patient information, even if it never sees a card number. Thus, the same page sits inside both scopes simultaneously. Assessment frequency The next difference between HIPAA and PCI is how often they expect you to review your security controls and scan your environment. PCI draws a minimum expectation of quarterly vulnerability scans and annual assessments. Along with that, it requires you to periodically pen-test your environment, and under 11.6.1, continuously monitor payment pages for unauthorized changes and tampering. HIPAA requires ongoing risk analysis and periodic evaluations, but sets no fixed cadence. OCR expects updates when your environment or threat landscape changes. That mismatch can have repercussions for portals that are constantly evolving with UX updates, tag rotation, and the addition of new scripts by marketing. In that situation, you could still be satisfying the minimum criteria for PCI DSS, but due to the dynamic nature of the page, you could be failing both HIPAA and PCI for not detecting risks early. Breach notification HIPAA’s breach notification rule is statutory. And it gives you around sixty days from the moment you discover a breach to notify affected patients, HHS, and, in large incidents, the media. However, the anchor is when you discover the breach, or when you were reasonably supposed to discover it with well functioning compliance program. The only time you can cross that notification deadline without repercussions is when the number of affected people is less than 500. Beyond that, OCR has gone after entities for delays, treating each day past that deadline as its own separate violation. PCI notification is contractual, but no less serious. You need to notify your acquirer and payment brands promptly, cooperate in forensic investigations, or face escalating per-card fines and potential loss of processing privileges. In the end, both frameworks are governing the same page, but they’re not governing it the same way. Here’s a side-by-side look at where they diverge. Requirement Area HIPAA PCI DSS 4.0.1 Scope All PHI across the organization, including billing data, identifiers, and any tracker that touches patient information Cardholder data environment. But 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 pull all payment-page scripts into scope regardless of who hosts the card fields Technical Specificity Flexible, risk-based safeguards. You define the how. OCR judges the outcome Prescriptive and testable. Specific controls, specific cadences, specific evidence expected Script Monitoring Implicit via risk analysis and OCR tracking guidance. The obligation is there; the prescription isn’t Explicit. 6.4.3 requires script inventory and integrity checks. 11.6.1 requires tamper detection, at a minimum, weekly Assessment Frequency Ongoing, no fixed cadence. OCR expects updates when your environment or threat landscape changes Annual ROC or SAQ, quarterly vulnerability scans, periodic pen tests, recurring payment page tamper checks Breach Notification 60 days from discovery, or when you were reasonably supposed to discover it. Each day past that is a separate violation Contractual, driven by your acquirer and card brand scheme rules. Delays compound fines and risk processing privileges Vendor Agreements Business Associate Agreements covering permitted uses, breach notification, and downstream subcontractors Service provider agreements defining compliance responsibilities, AOC evidence, and incident cooperation Penalties Tiered civil penalties up to $1.9M per violation category annually, plus state AG actions and class-action exposure Contractual fines from card brands, per-card penalties post-breach, higher transaction fees, or loss of processing privileges The healthcare payment page problem When you watch what loads on the browser at run-time, you’ll see your portal’s own scripts, your payment gateway, and a dozen third-party calls to analytics platforms, tag managers, and advertising pixels, firing in the background as a patient navigates their bill. That becomes a problem when you factor in that these pages are often designed for the best UX possible. It opts for a flow that removes friction with one continuous process from authentication to payment. That means PHI and card data, the two most protected data types in the US, are side-by-side, on the same webpage. Every script that loaded into that session can see all of it. Tracking scripts create a dual violation risk A marketing pixel transmitting PHI to an advertising platform is a HIPAA violation. A skimming script exfiltrating card data from the same page is a PCI violation. On a healthcare payment page, both can happen simultaneously, triggered by the same JavaScript ecosystem, invisible to the same compliance teams. Tracking pixels, analytics SDKs, and tag manager scripts monitor how users move through billing portals. Which links they click, what amounts they see, how far they scroll, and sometimes what they type. Tools like Meta Pixel can capture URLs with query parameters that include account IDs or service types, page titles that reference conditions or departments, and form field values if configured to do so. iFrames don’t solve it either The assumption is that because the PSP hosts the card fields in an iframe, the payment page is effectively out of PCI scope. The reality is that other scripts on the page can still observe DOM changes, watch behavioral patterns, and scrape surrounding PHI regardless of where the card fields are hosted. In some cases, when the scripts that load at run-time can call compromised dependencies in a downstream attack. That malicious script can steal and skim data in unpredictable ways, by replacing the iFrames with malicious ones, capturing the keystrokes, and more. Configuration drifts Tags and pixels for marketing purposes can’t differentiate between PHI, cardholder data, or any other sensitive data in real time. Even when just set for high-level analytics, it captures what happens in the DOM and sends it to the third-party servers for analysis. Configuring them to not fire on certain pages, not record certain sessions, and not capture certain fields is possible. But those configurations drift over time as marketing rotates tags or vendors push updates. Without continuous monitoring, what was compliant on day one quietly stops being compliant as the page evolves around it. Unified compliance for payment pages In the span of a single page load, patients enter their name, their account number, their diagnosis code, and their credit card. Two federal frameworks govern that moment. When two separate teams work in silos, neither team’s scope gets drawn to include what the other is watching. Scripts that touch PHI get reviewed for payment security. Trackers that sit on payment pages get reviewed for privacy risk. That’s a gap. A patient billing page is not a HIPAA asset that sometimes processes payments, and happens to display some health information. It is for every session. That means: Scoping billing and payment pages as part of the PHI environment under HIPAA risk analysis and Security Rule safeguards. scoping them as in-scope payment pages under PCI DSS 4.0.1, with full 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 coverage, including referring pages and single-page application views that load payment fields dynamically. Defaulting to a stricter standard leaves blindspots The instinct to default to whichever framework is more demanding sounds reasonable. But it falls apart in practice, as both frameworks are stricter in different areas. PCI DSS is strict on run-time governance. HIPAA is stricter on everything that counts as regulated health data. That means payment-related billing identifiers, account numbers, service descriptions, and procedure codes are all PHI under HIPAA’s broad definition. PCI’s scope stops at cardholder data. If you lean on PCI’s narrower data lens, you are under-classifying the information your payment page actually handles. Vendor agreements should be unified, too Any vendor that can see both patient information and card data in the same browser session needs to be treated as both a business associate and a PCI service provider. If your contracts do not reflect that, your risk register won’t stand scrutiny. For portal and UI platform vendors, that means a BAA that explicitly covers ePHI in the portal, Security Rule safeguard obligations, and breach notification responsibilities to you. It also means a PCI service provider agreement that defines their 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 responsibilities, evidence expectations, and roles in incident response. One contract or the other is not enough. You need both. How feroot enables dual compliance The tools most healthcare organizations rely on today were built for a threat model that starts at the server. WAFs protect the network perimeter. SIEM platforms aggregate server-side logs. Vulnerability scanners assess infrastructure. None of them see what executes inside the browser, which scripts load on a payment page, what data they access, and where they send it. That is the gap Feroot is built to close. Feroot delivers continuous run-time visibility It automatically discovers every script executing on payment pages and maps it directly to PCI DSS 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 requirements. As scripts get discovered, it maintains the inventory, enforces authorization workflows, and monitors continuously for drifts or behavioural changes, constantly verifying their integrity. When something on the payment page shifts, the platform detects it, flags it, and produces the audit-ready evidence QSAs expect. Feroot monitors the browser environment for PHI exposure AI automatically identifies PHI across web forms, medical search queries, and appointment scheduling systems, and maps every location where tracking technologies could access protected health information. This way, it alerts and blocks when data moves out to unauthorized third-party destinations via tracking scripts. With a unified, centralized inventory, BAAs get streamlined, and documentation gets simplified. Together, these tools cover the entire surface needed to satisfy PCI and HIPAA compliance. The bottom line Healthcare payment pages sit at the intersection of two regulatory frameworks, and managing them as separate programs leaves the most dangerous surface ungoverned. Securing that data requires a compliance posture that covers both.
